title: Curie-Weiss cell fluid model: Fitting to experimental critical-point data
authors: I. V. Pylyuk, O. A. Dobush, M. P. Kozlovskii, R. V. Romanik, M. A. Shpot
abstract: We examine how the Curie--Weiss cell fluid model can be quantitatively related to real fluids by determining its microscopic parameters from experimental critical-point data for water, carbon dioxide, and three polyol ester lubricants (POE5, POE7, and POE9). The microscopic parameters of the model are determined from the experimental values of the critical temperature and critical density: the global attraction coupling constant is fixed by the critical temperature, and the cell volume by the critical density. The critical pressure then follows as an independent model prediction, deviating from experimental values by 10--41$\%$ across the studied substances. Varying the ratio of local repulsion to global attraction $f=J_2/J_1$ over a wide range has only a weak effect on this deviation. For $f\geq1$, the model's critical compressibility factor lays within a narrow range $Z_c\approx0.382-0.386$, remaining close to the mean-field van der Waals value $Z_c=3/8=0.375$ and consistently overestimating experimental values. The best agreement with experiment is obtained for the polyol ester lubricants and improves along the POE5--POE7--POE9 series with increasing molar mass, suggesting that multiple-occupancy cell fluid models are well suited to systems of large molecules, particularly soft-matter systems with bounded interaction potentials. We further show that generalizing the model by introducing a temperature- and phase-dependent effective attraction allows it to describe a triple point and to reproduce the broad range of critical-to-triple temperature ratios $T_c/T_{\mathrm{tr}}$ characteristic of real fluids.
summary: This work applies the Curie-Weiss cell fluid model to analyze the critical and triple point behavior of various real fluids, including water and polyol esters. By fitting microscopic parameters to experimental critical data, the authors demonstrate the model's quantitative success, particularly for soft-matter systems, and show how it can be extended to describe complex phase transitions.
main_problem: The paper aims to establish a quantitative link between the microscopic parameters of the Curie-Weiss cell fluid model and the macroscopic critical and triple point data of real fluids.
main_result: The model shows the best quantitative agreement with polyol ester lubricants, suggesting its suitability for soft-matter systems, and can be generalized to describe the triple point by introducing temperature-dependent attraction.
method: The authors determine microscopic parameters by matching the model's predictions for critical temperature and density to experimental values, and then analyze deviations in critical pressure and compressibility factor.
model_or_system: The core model is the Curie-Weiss cell fluid model, characterized by interaction constants ($J_1$ for attraction, $J_2$ for repulsion) and cell volume ($v$). It is tested against critical-point data for water, $	ext{CO}_2$, and polyol ester lubricants.
key_observables: Critical temperature ($T_c$), critical density ($ho_c$), critical pressure ($P_c$), and the critical compressibility factor ($Z_c$).
important_parameters: The ratio of local repulsion to global attraction ($f=J_2/J_1$), and temperature-dependent attraction parameters ($\alpha_I, \alpha_{II}, \alpha_{III}$) for triple point analysis.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on matching the model to critical coordinates, and the basic model is noted to deviate from experiment, especially for water, due to neglecting specific interactions.
figures_summary: The notes mention figures illustrating the phase diagram with coexistence lines and the critical/triple points, and tables comparing calculated vs. experimental critical parameters.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by first fixing model parameters using $T_c$ and $ho_c$, analyzing the resulting $P_c$ and $Z_c$ deviations, and finally generalizing the model by introducing temperature-dependent attraction to describe the triple point behavior.
why_interesting: While focused on classical fluid thermodynamics, the methodology of mapping complex many-body interactions onto a simplified, parameterized model framework is relevant for understanding effective Hamiltonians in quantum many-body systems.
